blurb: A fifteenth-century Jaina answer to Kālidāsa's Kumārasambhava. Where Kālidāsa tells of the birth of Kumāra (Kārttikeya), Jayaśekharasūri tells of the birth of Bharata, son of Ṛṣabhadeva. On the way the poem describes Ayodhyā, Ṛṣabha's birth and youth, his marriage to Sumaṅgalā and Sunandā, the fourteen dreams, the seasons and the dawn. It runs to eleven sargas and is printed with the ṭīkā of the poet's pupil Dharmaśekharasūri.
about: According to the commentator, Sarasvatī appeared to Jayaśekharasūri while he sat in meditation at Stambhatīrtha (Khambhat). She gave him the two opening verses, astyuttarasyāṃ diśi kośaleti and sampannakāmā nayanābhirāmāḥ, and asked him to compose the rest. The poet calls himself vāṇīdattavaraḥ in the last verse of the final sarga.

Dharmaśekharasūri's ṭīkā is deliberately simple. It opens each verse with a pratīka, restores prose word order, glosses words with synonyms and names figures of speech such as utprekṣā and virodha. It also cites Hemacandra's Siddhahema for grammatical points.
The 1946 edition was begun by Ācārya Vijayakṣamābhadrasūri, who died after eight sargas had been printed. Muni Vikramavijaya completed it from sarga 9 onward using the same press copy.

blurb: Jinasena's life of Pārśvanātha, the 23rd Tīrthaṅkara, woven around Kālidāsa's Meghadūta. Every one of the Meghadūta's lines is taken up as a samasyā and completed into a new verse, so the demon Śambara's assault on the meditating Pārśva is told in the cadence of the yakṣa's message to the cloud. The poem has four sargas and 364 verses, almost all in mandākrāntā.
about: Jinasena uses the samasyāpūraṇa technique throughout. He takes a line of the Meghadūta unchanged and composes the rest of the verse around it. Usually the borrowed line is the fourth, but it can be the first, second or third, and in 117 verses two lines are taken. Across 358 verses all 480 lines of Kālidāsa's 120 verses are used. The last six verses of sarga 4 are Jinasena's own conclusion, in other metres.

Because a samasyā must keep the borrowed line intact, scholars since K. B. Pathak have used the Pārśvābhyudaya as a witness to the Meghadūta as it was read in the ninth century. The reader marks each borrowed line in the verse and rebuilds the Meghadūta from them in the order Jinasena uses them.
The colophons call each of the four sargas bhagavatkaivalyavarṇana, and the source notes that it is unclear why they all share this name.
